title: Finding setups before the move - not just stocks that have already run
author: One-Cellist-8159
selftext:
One thing that frustrates me about trading tools: they’re great at showing you what already moved. Finding something worth researching *before* the obvious breakout or breakdown is harder.

I’ve been thinking about this more with the possibility of lower S&P 500 returns over the next decade. Nobody knows how that plays out, but even a sluggish index can hide very different opportunities underneath.

That’s part of why I built **EdgeCipher’s Market Intelligence module**. It’s a visual way to explore where potential accumulation or distribution pressure is developing across the market and identify individual stocks worth a closer look - on both the bullish and bearish sides.

Some names it’s currently putting on my research list:

* **Bearish setups to investigate:** DIS, SNDK
* **Bullish setups to investigate:** BA, PEG, FDX, PKG, UNH, WELL, AMAT, QCOM

These aren’t automatic buy or short calls. They’re starting points for research, confirmation, and risk planning. A developing setup can fail, and inferred accumulation/distribution isn’t proof of what institutions are doing.

The goal is simple: **spend less time searching and more time evaluating a manageable list of potential setups.**

On this page, it will be very easy to look at relative performance of different sectors [https://edgecipher.ai/market-stream](https://edgecipher.ai/market-stream)

Full disclosure: I’m the builder. If this sounds useful, you can check it out at [**EdgeCipher.ai**](http://edgecipher.ai/) . I’d genuinely appreciate feedback, especially from part-time swing traders.

**What’s harder for you: finding a setup early, or deciding whether it’s worth taking?**

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Finding things before the move is the right problem, but it's also the easiest one to fool yourself on, because any list looks smart after the fact. The way to find out if the module adds anything is to log every name it flags with the date, then check what each did over the next 5, 20 and 60 days against the S&P 500 and against a random list of the same size, keeping the ones that failed in the record. Accumulation and distribution from price and volume is an inference, as you say, so I'd also see how often a flagged name was just a stock that had already moved, since that's the thing you're trying to avoid. Cymetica's Event Cards are one place to browse event markets tied to scheduled dates like earnings, which often decide whether a setup works.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: A public track record is the right thing to share. Since you changed how the list and strategies are generated in July, I'd treat the results before and after that date as two separate records and judge the newer one on its own. Check that each pick is time-stamped when it was flagged and that returns are compared against the S&P 500 and a random list of the same size, including the losers. Thanks for sharing it.

comments.author: investigatormaker
comments.body:
On your closing question, the second half is where a list like this lives or dies: a part-time swing trader can't easily judge ten names without a track record. A dated public log of each past list, with what every name did over the following weeks, would be the outside check, and it's the clearest way to show whether the module flags setups before the move. Showing per ticker which signal put it there would also help someone with an hour after work decide whether it's worth a closer look.
